overview: The MPS School Committee is the governing body for Medford Public Schools, responsible for district policy, budget approval, and the oversight of the superintendent. Since late 2022, the committee has managed significant transitions in leadership and prioritized long-term infrastructure planning. Its primary focus involves navigating a multi-year project with the Massachusetts School Building Authority (MSBA) to renovate or rebuild the high school complex. As of October 2026, the body is engaged in implementing a district-wide strategic plan while executing large-scale HVAC and roof repairs across its elementary and middle school facilities.

threads.name: High School Building Project (MSBA)
threads.summary: The committee initiated a resubmission to the MSBA core project program in early 2023 to address facility needs at Medford High School. Following acceptance into the eligibility phase, the body formed a dedicated building committee and secured community members and professional consultants to lead a feasibility study. By 2026, the committee had narrowed down dozens of design alternatives to six preferred options, including renovation and new construction models. The project recently navigated property deed restrictions on Edgerly Field and submitted a preliminary design program to state authorities.

threads.name: District Safety and Security
threads.summary: Following a stabbing at the high school in December 2022, the committee pivoted toward intensive safety reviews and the implementation of a 10-point action plan. This plan introduced hallway monitoring, bathroom occupancy limits, and anonymous reporting systems. The body also engaged external consultants to review school climate and disciplinary enforcement. Recent security work has expanded to include the installation of district-wide security cameras and vape detectors funded through capital appropriations.

threads.name: Facilities and HVAC Infrastructure
threads.summary: The district faced widespread cooling and heating system failures starting in 2023, prompting a series of large-scale capital projects. The committee approved a $25 million bond for comprehensive HVAC replacements at the McGlynn and Andrews schools to address obsolete refrigerants and failing equipment. Subsequent repair projects were authorized for Roberts and Missituk Elementary schools, including transitions to geothermal and air-source heat pump systems. The body also established a recurring capital plan to track roof replacements and ADA accessibility needs across all five campuses.

threads.name: Elementary Overcrowding and Space Planning
threads.summary: By late 2024, critical overcrowding at Roberts Elementary prompted the committee to explore redistricting and space utilization models. The body approved the relocation of preschool classrooms to other schools to create immediate space while commissioning a formal facilities utilization study. A proposal to restructure K-8 schools into specialized grade spans was tabled to allow for more public input. The committee ultimately decided to delay any major middle school grade reconfigurations until at least 2028 to align with future construction timelines.

threads.name: Budget and Financial Strategy
threads.summary: The committee managed a $2.5 million projected shortfall in fiscal year 2024 through spending freezes and grant reallocations. To achieve long-term stability, the body formally supported local tax override ballot questions in late 2024 to fund city and school operations. These funds were later used to restore literacy coaches, behavioral specialists, and other staff positions previously cut. The committee also established a special education reserve fund and adopted a new eight-phase budget schedule to increase transparency and community participation.

threads.name: Curriculum and Graduation Standards
threads.summary: A multi-year review of literacy instruction led to the adoption of a new district-wide elementary curriculum aligned with the science of reading. Following state-level changes to MCAS graduation requirements, the committee updated district policy to ensure graduation is determined by the successful completion of coursework rather than standardized test scores. The body also piloted integrated mathematics pathways and developed a district-wide instructional vision centered on equity and data-informed practices.

threads.name: Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion
threads.summary: The committee established comprehensive policies regarding gender identity non-discrimination, ensuring student access to appropriate facilities and the use of preferred pronouns. The body also ratified resolutions affirming support for LGBTQIA+ students and revised Title IX grievance procedures to comply with updated federal regulations. Discussions regarding a dedicated district-level DEI director led to a temporary compensation agreement with the city's DEI director while the committee explored creating a permanent school-based position.

periods.narrative: This term was defined by a major crisis response following a high school stabbing and the subsequent development of safety protocols and a 10-point action plan.
This period focused on navigating a severe budget deficit, securing a municipal tax override, and launching massive HVAC replacement projects for the middle and elementary schools.
The current term is centered on stabilizing district leadership with a permanent superintendent appointment and finalizing design plans for the MSBA high school project.
